records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client-side rejectedEmails check compares the raw typed string against the server-returned rejected email, but the server-side uniqueness/presence checks and BlockedEmail lookup are case-insensitive at the DB level (MySQL/PG citext or lower-case comparisons vary), and an email rejected once is rejected for exact matches only. A user whose 'User@Spam.com' was rejected gets the instant inline 'invalid' message when retyping the identical string, but changing case ('user@spam.com') bypasses the client check and resubmits to the server, producing a flash error instead of inline feedback — inconsistent UX, and the property dependency `rejectedEmails.@each` correctly re-fires only for the exact string.

records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail lookup compares email case-sensitively (where(email: email) on Postgres) while the blocked list is loaded by hand with no canonicalization, and no downcase is applied on either write or read. An operator inserting 'Spam@Example.com' into blocked_emails (the only population path) never matches a user registering 'spam@example.com', so the block silently fails; the unique index likewise permits 'a@x.com' and 'A@x.com' as distinct blocked rows.
records.rationale: Verified in diff: `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` does an exact match lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) with no normalization on read or write, and the migration adds a plain unique index on `:email` (`add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true`). Since no `downcase`/canonicalization (or `citext` / functional index) is applied anywhere in `BlockedEmail` or `EmailValidator`, case-variant emails like `Spam@Example.com` vs `spam@example.com` can fail to match and can coexist as distinct rows, making blocking unreliable.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The email validator (including the blocked-email check) only runs when email_changed?, and only on the User model — no other email-ingestion path validates. Invites, admin-created users via other flows, or email updates that dodge email_changed? bypass the blocked list entirely; parallel service paths mean blocked emails can still enter the system through invite-based signup, which creates a User without running this validation chain in the same way.

A spammer blocked as 'bad@spammers.org' registers as 'Bad@Spammers.ORG' and passes the new 'blocked' validation that this PR's whole purpose is to enforce; the check intended to stop them returns false and the account is created.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The email uniqueness validation is now a plain Rails uniqueness check with no case-insensitive scope or downcasing, combined with the removal of the dedicated email_validator method means case-variant duplicate emails are never blocked at the app layer. If the DB unique index on users.email is case-sensitive (Postgres default), 'Bob@x.com' and 'bob@x.com' both validate as unique, producing duplicate accounts for one mailbox — an account-recovery/impersonation foothold for shared-mailbox domains; the index schema is not added or altered in this diff to enforce case-insensitivity.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The failure response now echoes user-supplied values (name, username, email) back in the JSON payload, which the client pushes into client-side state and re-displays via the error flash path. Any XSS sink that renders result.values.email or the flash message without escaping turns the signup form into a reflected/stored XSS vector via the server-echoed email field; safe only as long as every consuming template escapes, which this diff does not verify.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The match_count increment uses read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1; record.save) with no locking, so concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked email lose increments. Operators relying on match_count to gauge spam pressure under-count under concurrency (two simultaneous requests both read count=5, both write 6); also the concurrent saves can collide on updated_at/last_match_at, last write wins. Low impact for stats, but the counter's purpose (measuring abuse volume) is exactly the workload where concurrency occurs.
records.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the diff explicitly increments via read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1` then `record.save`). Under concurrent calls for the same email, both requests can read the same `match_count` and write back the same incremented value, losing an update; similarly `last_match_at` is overwritten by the last writer. This makes the persisted counter/statistics incorrect under concurrency, matching the finding’s mechanism.
